SUSTAINABLE SPECIES IN THE ARCTIC

Shared worlds.
Different perspectives.

How can we create sustainable futures for humans and other species in a rapidly changing Arctic?

SPECIES explores environmental conflicts involving humans and other species across Norway, Finland and Greenland.

Climate change, conservation policies, infrastructure and competing demands on resources are reshaping Arctic relationships. These changes raise questions about sustainability, Indigenous rights, traditional livelihoods and how different species can continue to live together.

Different ways of understanding a shared world

Environmental conflicts concern more than wildlife or resources. They involve cultural practices, relationships between beings and the authority to decide how environments should be managed.

Through the concept of multispecies ontologies, the project explores different understandings of animals, humans and landscapes. It brings scientific, local and Indigenous perspectives into dialogue without assuming they should be reduced to a single framework.

How we work

Anthropology, biology, ecology, genetics, technology studies and audio-visual art contribute methods suited to each case. Depending on the setting, these include participant observation, interviews, scientific data collection, genetic analysis, drone testing and ecological modelling.

Collaborative fieldwork and participatory workshops create opportunities to exchange knowledge, identify shared goals and connect research with local priorities. Local and Indigenous partners participate in framing questions as well as developing knowledge.

Questions guiding the research

  • How can environmental conflicts be co-researched through different multispecies ontologies?
  • How can local and Indigenous knowledge work alongside research to question approaches to development, management and conservation?
  • How can participatory fieldwork and Indigenous methodologies challenge reductive understandings of traditional knowledge?
  • How can co-producing knowledge advance sustainable multispecies relations?

Towards sustainable multispecies futures

The project seeks to strengthen collaboration, identify shared priorities and explore culturally sensitive approaches to environmental management. Its ambition is to build alliances that recognise local aspirations, Indigenous sovereignty and the value of different knowledge traditions.

Three regional work packages

WP1 — Sápmi, Norway
Reindeer herding and technology; king crab fisheries and international markets.
WP2 — Finland
Baltic sealing traditions and marine relations; Lapland cattle, genetic heritage and agriculture.
WP3 — Greenland
Polar bears, predation and food security; muskoxen, changing ecologies and coexistence.

Wild ducks and Sámi artistic collaboration are also part of the seven-species project overview. The supplied work-package list does not separately assign that case.

Partners shaping the research

Workshops led by local and Indigenous partners provide opportunities to frame questions, exchange knowledge and identify shared goals. The project asks how research can respect the worldviews and practices through which knowledge is formed, and address inequalities between communities, researchers, industry and the state.
